title: Why Antonelli’s title win is an explosive shot in the arm for F1
excerpt:
In the first four years of the Formula 1 World Championship, Italians were crowned champion three times. The first, in 1950, was the patrician Dr Giuseppe Farina; he was followed by the great Alberto Ascari in 1952 and 1953.

But it was not until November 1, 2026, in Mexico City that 20-year-old non-pareil Kimi Antonelli finally ended Italy’s 73-year drought to become their next champion.

That’s an awful long time between dances. And in doing so he joined another rare club, populated by Juan Manuel Fangio, Jacques Villeneuve and Lewis Hamilton, previously the only men to have donned the crown in only their second season in F1.

title: Antonelli shares touching reaction to ‘incredible’ title win
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has reacted to winning his maiden World Championship at the Mexico City Grand Prix, with the Italian hiding none of his emotions as he thanked those around him for an “incredible season”.

Although it was Red Bull’s Max Verstappen who won the race ahead of Lewis Hamilton, Antonelli’s P3 finish earned him more than enough points to clinch the title, joining the likes of the Ferrari driver, Graham Hill, and Denny Hulme in doing so at this circuit.

After starting from fourth on the grid, the 20-year-old improved to the top three via a bold overtake on Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, which allowed him to celebrate his historic victory on the podium after embracing his family and Mercedes team members.

“We did it,” Antonelli said after the race. “You know, without them, I wouldn’t be here – without Mercedes, without my family. So I’m very grateful for this moment, and it’s one that will live forever. I’m speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened.

“It’s been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max and Lewis is truly incredible. And yeah, looking forward to some more battles in the future.

“This weekend I did feel a bit more tense, but I’m just so happy, and happy that we got it done, and now we can enjoy the rest of the season.”

Antonelli has not only become the sport’s youngest-ever World Champion, but also Italy’s first in 73 years after he netted 380 points over 19 rounds, which those behind him are mathematically unable to surpass in the season’s remaining events.

Reflecting further on his immense achievement, he added: “[It’s] a moment that means so much. It’s a day I will remember forever. Thank you so much to my team, my family, my friends, and all of you guys that support me and the sport. I’m just so grateful.

“Very early on, we had such a strong car, and we were very consistent and put in the performance. I thought that we could have had a shot this year, and I’m really happy that we managed to clinch it all.

“It’s starting to get real, and I’m going to enjoy every bit of it. I mean, I’m going to go all out, right? I’m going to go all out with my family, friends, and the team. And we’re just going to enjoy it all the way, because this is a very special moment, one that we’ll remember forever.”

title: Antonelli crowned champion in Mexico as Verstappen wins race
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli became the youngest ever Formula 1 World Champion as third place in the Mexico City Grand Prix was enough for the Mercedes driver to claim the 2026 crown, with Max Verstappen taking race victory from Lewis Hamilton.

Antonelli entered Sunday's 71-lap race at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez needing only to finish ninth to claim a maiden F1 title, regardless of where rivals Hamilton and Mercedes team mate George Russell finished.

The 20-year-old started fourth and eventually finished third in a race where the Italian had to deal with a mid-race red flag after a heavy accident for Valtteri Bottas and a late Safety Car following a crash for Arvid Lindblad.

Out in front, Verstappen claimed his third win of the season, the Red Bull driver withstanding late pressure from Hamilton to claim an unlikely win from fifth on the grid after being helped by an intense Ferrari intra-team battle.

Having jumped up to second on the opening lap, Verstappen took the lead after Charles Leclerc was handed a time penalty for cutting the track on the first lap when battling polesitter Hamilton.

The Dutchman then held the lead at the standing restart and maintained the lead again after the Safety Car was recalled with eight laps remaining, with Hamilton a constant threat.

Leclerc finished fourth after withstanding immense late pressure from Lando Norris' McLaren, with George Russell (Mercedes), Oscar Piastri (McLaren), Franco Colapinto (Alpine), Liam Lawson's Racing Bulls from the pit lane and the second Alpine of Pierre Gasly completing the top 10.

Gabriel Bortoleto was P11 for Audi, ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar who was tipped into a spin by Russell on the opening lap, with Ryo Hirakawa finishing P13 for Haas on his F1 debut after a mid-weekend call-up.

Alex Albon headed Williams team mate Carlos Sainz, Nico Hulkenberg was P16 after a 10-second penalty for a collision with Ollie Bearman ahead of home hero Sergio Perez, the Cadillac driver the last of the classified runners.

Lindblad crashed out at Turn 2 after a late collision with Piastri, Bearman retired after contact from Hulkenberg, while Bottas and the two Aston Martins of Lance Stroll and Fernando Alonso retired.

AS IT HAPPENED

Drivers faced the longest run of the season down to the first corner at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez once the red lights went out, with Hamilton holding his pole position advantage and leading a line of cars into the braking zone.

The seven-time World Champion immediately faced pressure from his Ferrari team mate, though, Leclerc diving to the outside as the pair ran side-by-side through the opening turns with Hamilton just holding the advantage.

The Briton went defensive again into Turn 4, with Leclerc sweeping to the outside as the pair went side-by-side into the braking zone once more.

Both went off track and just avoided contact, with Leclerc deciding to head across the grass to take the lead, while Hamilton rejoined the track but with a compromised exit through the right of Turn 5.

This allowed Verstappen to jump Hamilton on the exit and into the next corner, preventing any chance for Leclerc to give Hamilton the position back, while behind, Russell tapped Hadjar into a spin at Turn 6.

The Mercedes driver had started on the front row and initially challenged Hamilton on the run down to the first corner, but he was swamped before even reaching the braking zone due to apparent energy deployment issues and had dropped to P6 before the contact.

The incident between the Ferrari drivers was immediately placed under investigation, with Leclerc leading Verstappen, Hamilton, Antonelli and Russell, as Norris worked his way up to P6 after losing positions on the opening lap to Colapinto and Lindblad.

A brief Virtual Safety Car appeared on Lap 7, Stroll having pulled his Aston Martin off at Turn 6 as team mate Alonso retired in the pits to complete a miserable race for the team.

By Lap 12, Leclerc had pulled out a 3.2-second gap to Verstappen as the Monegasque driver was handed a 5s penalty for his opening lap incident with Hamilton, a 10s penalty not applied by the stewards as both drivers had gone off track. Russell, meanwhile, was handed 10s for his collision with Hadjar.

Unlike the rest of the leading runners on the soft Pirelli tyre, Verstappen had opted for the medium rubber and in theory a longer opening stint, the Dutchman maintaining a consistent two-second gap to Hamilton, with Antonelli a similar margin behind.

Russell, meanwhile, was dropping away and falling into the clutches of Norris, with Piastri, Lindblad, Colapinto and Hulkenberg on the medium tyre completing the top 10, followed by Audi team mate Bortoleto, Bearman and Gasly.

Home hero Perez found himself up in P14, heading both Williams, rookie Hirakawa, the recovering Hadjar who pitted under the VSC, Cadillac team mate Bottas and Lawson, the Racing Bulls driver having started from the pit lane after being disqualified from Qualifying.

Gasly stopped on Lap 17 for medium tyres, as Bearman jumped Bortoleto at Turn 1 for P11, the Haas driver having taken his best F1 result 12 months ago in Mexico with P4.

By the start of Lap 22, Leclerc held a 5s margin over Verstappen as clean air for the race leader was proving crucial, with Hamilton and Antonelli continuing to follow in the dirty air of Verstappen.

Hamilton made his feelings clear about Leclerc's penalty over the radio, stating "the stewards are basically handing Charles this win", having dropped 7.5s adrift by Lap 24.

Piastri became the first of the leading runners to pit at the end of Lap 26 from P7, switching from the soft to the medium tyre as the Australian struggled to match the pace of team mate Norris ahead having started P12.

It prompted a flurry of pit lane action, Leclerc and Verstappen both pitting the next lap and the Red Bull driver rejoining ahead as Leclerc served his penalty.

Leclerc was now on a medium and Verstappen on the soft, with the four-time World Champion told he would run to the end with more than 40 laps remaining.

Hamilton pitted the next lap for mediums, handing the lead to Antonelli, and he rejoined behind Verstappen and Leclerc, with Russell and Norris now P2 and P3 but also yet to stop.

Norris continued to challenge Russell, who was 5.6s behind Antonelli, but was unable to find a way through, having been told his best option was to stay out and hope for a Safety Car.

Norris was finally released as Russell pitted at the end of Lap 33, the Briton serving his 10s penalty and rejoining back in P8 and just ahead of Piastri, who had struggled to clear Bearman for several laps.

Lindblad made his sole stop from P6 two laps later, rejoining back in P10 and ahead of Hadjar with Bearman and Bortoleto up ahead also yet to pit.

By Lap 38, Antonelli held a 9s lead from Norris, who in turn was 3s clear of Verstappen, with Leclerc only 1.6s behind and Hamilton 2s back – the top five covered by nearly 15s.

But just a lap later Norris blinked, bringing his McLaren into the pits for a set of medium tyres, the reigning World Champion who was on the brink of relinquishing his crown rejoining in a lonely P5 after a slow stop.

With 30 laps remaining, Verstappen had closed to within 9.4s of Antonelli, with Leclerc in third and complaining his car was difficult to drive.

Bearman pitted from P8 and rejoined P14 on the medium tyre, with Hadjar making his second stop a lap later and finding himself in P15.

Antonelli also headed for the pits on Lap 43, the final driver to make a tyre change and rejoining comfortably in P4 despite a 4.3-second stop just moments before a Safety Car was deployed.

Bottas suffered a heavy crash at Turn 1, the Finn finding the barrier after his front left suspension failed under braking, prompting Hamilton to pit, and dropping behind Antonelli, as did Russell and Piastri.

The Safety Car was upgraded to a red flag starting from Lap 46 due to barrier damage, while Bottas briefly received medical attention. Eventually extracting himself from the car unaided having been responsive on the radio, he was taken to the medical centre for precautionary checks.

Gasly was initially placed under investigation after the Alpine driver headed out of the pit lane just as the red light had appeared to neutralise the race, but the stewards took no further action due to the limited time to react.

Verstappen lined up for the standing restart at the head of the field from Leclerc, with Hamilton reinstated in P3 ahead of Antonelli, as Norris, Russell, Piastri, Lindblad, Colapinto and Gasly completed the top 10, all fitted with soft tyres.

As the red lights went out for the second time, Hamilton immediately jumped ahead of Leclerc off the line and challenged Verstappen into Turn 1, moving to the outside but running out of room and having to slot back into second after the pair made minor contact.

Leclerc lost another position the following lap into Turn 1, Antonelli diving to the inside before the Ferrari driver had to continually defend from Norris over the closing stages and complaining about vibrations after a huge lock-up into the opening corner at the restart.

As Bearman retired in the pits after a collision with Hulkenberg at Turn 4, which earned the Audi driver a 10s penalty, Hamilton continued to hustle Verstappen as Antonelli closed on the pair.

Verstappen was placed under investigation for a potential out of position start, which was eventually dismissed, as was any action after his Turn 1 moment with Hamilton.

A late Safety Car was deployed after Piastri and Lindblad came together through the opening sequence of corners, the McLaren driver on the outside of Turn 1 and clipping the right-rear of the Racing Bulls machine, with the contact sending the rookie into the wall.

Verstappen nailed the restart with eight laps remaining, and despite Hamilton looming large, held on to win by 0.7s, as Antonelli completed the podium just 4s adrift on a weekend to remember for the young Italian.

Key quote

"We did it. And, you know, without them, I wouldn’t be here. Without Mercedes, without my family," said new World Champion Kimi Antonelli. "So I’m very grateful for this moment, and it’s one that will live forever. And I just, I’m speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened."

What's next

You might think a man with 104 pole positions would not be too excited about one more, but Lewis Hamilton – never one to hide his mood – was bouncing up and down with joy at the conclusion of Qualifying yesterday, much like he did 20 seasons ago, when bagging his first.

No.105 has been a long time coming. His first for Ferrari, three years and a team change after his last for Mercedes.

The good news for Hamilton in his quest for victory is that practice suggested overtaking in Sunday's race is going to be very difficult. The bad news is that it’s an awfully long way to Turn 1, and he’s going to be towing a pack of highly motivated rivals all the way down to the braking point.

George Russell starts P2, with Charles Leclerc and Kimi Antonelli on the second row, while Max Verstappen and Lando Norris are on row three. The race is tantalisingly poised between one stop and two, which is going to make it very interesting indeed.

title: How F1 drivers and teams have embraced Dia de Muertos
excerpt:
The Mexico City Grand Prix is renowned for its passionate crowds, colourful paddock and spectacular celebrations. But this year, the race takes place during one of Mexico's most important cultural occasions – Dia de Muertos, or Day of the Dead.

Taking place around the beginning of November, Dia de Muertos is a time for families to remember loved ones who have passed away and is traditionally marked through decorated altars, food, flowers and celebrations that bring communities together.

For Formula 1, the celebration has become a familiar part of its annual visit to the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez. Drivers have embraced the occasion through special helmets, elaborate face paint and even cooking challenges, while the paddock has welcomed performers and displays inspired by Mexican traditions.

As the 2026 race weekend coincides with Dia de Muertos, here's a closer look at the celebration, the meanings behind its most recognisable customs and how they have made their mark on F1.

What is Dia de Muertos?

Although its name might suggest otherwise, Dia de Muertos is as much a celebration of life as it is a remembrance of death. Rooted in pre-Hispanic traditions that later became intertwined with Catholic observances introduced by the Spanish, the celebration centres on the belief that deceased loved ones can temporarily return to the world of the living. While customs differ between communities, 1 November is commonly associated with remembering children who have passed, while 2 November is dedicated to deceased adults.

Rather than being an occasion solely for mourning, Dia de Muertos provides families with an opportunity to reconnect with those they have lost through their favourite foods, personal belongings and shared memories. Homes and cemeteries are typically decorated with flowers, candles and offerings, while relatives gather to celebrate the lives of their loved ones. Its cultural significance was recognised by UNESCO when the tradition was proclaimed in 2003, before being inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008.

When Dia de Muertos inspires the drivers' helmets

Special helmets have become a regular feature of the Mexico City Grand Prix, with drivers using the occasion to incorporate Mexican artwork into their designs.

In 2024, Carlos Sainz unveiled a Dia de Muertos-inspired helmet featuring a colourful skull motif across the crown. The design also incorporated a chilli pepper, referencing his long-standing nickname. The Spaniard went on to win the race for Ferrari, making it a memorable helmet for his collection.

Sainz was not the only driver incorporating the occasion into his race weekend that year, with Pierre Gasly also opting for a special design featuring Dia de Muertos-inspired imagery. However, few drivers have embraced Mexican heritage through their helmet designs as consistently as Sergio Perez.

For his home race in 2022, the Red Bull driver unveiled a design featuring La Catrina, an elegantly dressed skeletal figure who has become one of the most recognisable symbols associated with the festivities. The helmet also incorporated papel picado, the decorative paper banners traditionally created by cutting intricate patterns into sheets of coloured tissue paper.

La Catrina has a fascinating history of her own. The figure emerged through the work of Mexican printmaker Jose Guadalupe Posada, whose satirical skeletal imagery was later popularised by the artist Diego Rivera. Today, she appears throughout Dia de Muertos celebrations, with her distinctive hat and elaborate clothing inspiring everything from face paint to enormous public installations.

The following year, Perez unveiled another helmet created by Mexican artist Karla Lozano, whose winning design incorporated papel picado, alebrijes and other cultural references to Mexico and his home state of Jalisco. While alebrijes belong to a wider tradition of Mexican folk art, they have also become familiar sights at contemporary Dia de Muertos celebrations.

The paddock gets a Dia de Muertos makeover

Over the years, the Mexico City Grand Prix paddock has become almost as colourful as the celebrations taking place across the capital.

Anyone who remembers the 2016 Mexico City Grand Prix might recall a rather unusual appearance by Red Bull team mates Max Verstappen and Daniel Ricciardo. Arriving for their Thursday media commitments, the pair were almost unrecognisable beneath elaborate skull-inspired face paint, embracing the imagery associated with Dia de Muertos. Mercedes also joined in with the festivities that year, decorating their hospitality area to mark the occasion.

The colourful skeletal designs worn by the Red Bull drivers echoed the calavera, or skull, imagery commonly seen during Dia de Muertos. Skulls appear in various forms during Día de Muertos, including decorative artwork, face paint and sugar skulls known as calaveras de azucar.

The tradition has continued at subsequent races. In 2024, drivers entering the paddock were welcomed by performers dressed as Catrinas, who handed out cempasuchil flowers, the bright orange Mexican marigolds closely associated with Dia de Muertos. Charles Leclerc made a particularly memorable entrance in a traditional charro-style outfit associated with mariachi musicians, carrying one of the flowers given to him on arrival.

Cempasuchil flowers are traditionally used to help guide the spirits of deceased loved ones back to their families, with petals often arranged along pathways leading towards altars.

A taste of Mexico

Food is central to Dia de Muertos, and it has also provided Formula 1 drivers with some rather entertaining experiences away from the track. During the 2024 Mexico City Grand Prix weekend, Oscar Piastri swapped racing duties for food preparation, making guacamole alongside a Dia de Muertos performer in the paddock.

While guacamole itself is not specific to the celebration, food plays an important role in Dia de Muertos, with families preparing dishes enjoyed by deceased relatives and placing them on ofrendas.

These offerings vary depending on the individual being remembered and the traditions of each family, with everything from tamales and mole to fruit, sweets and favourite drinks appearing alongside photographs and personal possessions.

Perhaps the most recognisable seasonal speciality is pan de muerto, a traditional sweet bread prepared around Dia de Muertos. Often flavoured with orange blossom or citrus and topped with sugar, some versions feature dough decorations shaped to resemble bones.

Recipes differ across Mexico, with regional varieties and contemporary fillings adding to the range available in bakeries during October and November. This year, the Mexico City Grand Prix organisers have confirmed that visitors will be able to sample different versions at the circuit, including traditional sugar-coated breads and filled alternatives.

Ofrendas and the meaning behind the celebrations

While the colourful costumes, special helmets and paddock activities have become familiar features of the Mexico City Grand Prix, one of the central Dia de Muertos traditions is the ofrenda.

These altars, created in homes, cemeteries and public spaces, are dedicated to deceased loved ones, bringing together photographs, personal belongings and offerings that reflect the lives of those being remembered.

For the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix, organisers have confirmed that an altar de muertos will be installed in the circuit's Blue Zone, dedicated to members of the motorsport community who have passed away.

It marks a particularly poignant addition to this year's race weekend, offering a connection between Mexico's tradition of remembrance and the people who have helped shape the sport's history.

With the Grand Prix taking place on 1 November, the display also serves as a reminder of the significance behind the festivities that have become such a recognisable part of F1's annual visit. Beyond the elaborate artwork and celebrations, Dia de Muertos remains an occasion for honouring those who are no longer here, ensuring their memories continue to be shared.

title: Furious Ferrari boss lays into Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc for 'lack of respect'
excerpt:
A furious Fred Vasseur has accused Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc of showing a "lack of respect" to Ferrari following their Mexico City GP clash.

Hamilton started on pole in Mexico and was primed to tow Leclerc from third down to Turn 1, with the latter moving to the outside of the turn to move up the inside of Turn 2, with Hamilton ahead on the run to Turn 4.

There, Leclerc attempted to swing around the outside, with both he and Hamilton running off the track, as Leclerc got ahead by cutting the track, with Ferrari's misery then compounded by Max Verstappen getting ahead of Hamilton.

Leclerc was subsequently handed a five-second time penalty by the stewards for gaining a lasting advantage, with Hamilton remarking over the radio that the stewards had handed Leclerc a win by only giving him five seconds of penalty, as he still enjoyed clean air.

Verstappen got ahead through the pit-stops as Leclerc served his penalty, with the Red Bull fending off Hamilton's late pursuit through a second standing restart and safety car period to snatch the win - with Red Bull now holding three wins in 2026 to Ferrari's two.

Hamilton was second and Leclerc fourth - but post-race, a furious Vasseur tore into his drivers.

"I'm struggling to swallow it because, honestly, I think it's a lack of respect, a lack of respect for the brand, a lack of respect for all the people working here and for the efforts we're putting in," Vasseur told Canal+.

"We've taken a real step forward in terms of performance, and I think throwing away a win like that is tough."

When then asked if he was directly calling out Leclerc, Vasseur denied the Monegasque was the target of his frustrations and wanted to speak with both drivers.

"No, no, I didn't target anyone; I want to talk with them," he said.

"Lewis was running very wide too, but look, I think we also need to keep in mind that we represent a brand, we represent sponsors, we've got 2,000 people working behind us who aren't just racing for the sake of racing; they're racing for the whole team."

title: Kimi Antonelli title history hailed as 'only the beginning' of F1 legacy
excerpt:
Stefano Domenicali has declared that Kimi Antonelli's world championship marks the start of an "extraordinary legacy" after the Mercedes driver became Formula 1's youngest champion.

Antonelli sealed the 2026 drivers' title by finishing third in the Mexico City Grand Prix. The 20-year-old also becomes the first Italian to win the championship since Alberto Ascari in 1953, ending a 73-year wait for the country.

The Mercedes driver's rise has been rapid. Signed to the Brackley-based squad's junior programme back in 2019, Antonelli was fast-tracked straight into Formula 2 for 2024, skipping Formula 3 entirely, before stepping into a Mercedes race seat in 2025.

F1 CEO Domenicali framed Antonelli's achievement as historic on multiple fronts.

"Today, Kimi Antonelli has made history," said Domenicali. "Becoming the youngest F1 world champion is an extraordinary achievement, earned through exceptional talent, courage and determination."

"It fills me with immense pride to see Kimi become the first Italian Formula 1 world champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953.

"For 73 years, our country has waited for this moment, and today an entire nation will celebrate one of its own reaching the very pinnacle of our sport."

[Article continues below]

Antonelli 'inspiring a generation'

Domenicali went on to tie Antonelli's achievement to its wider impact beyond the result itself.

"Greatness is measured not only by records, but by the generations it inspires," he added.

"Kimi has captured the imagination of millions of fans around the world and shown young people everywhere that there are no limits to what can be achieved through dedication, belief and hard work.

"Across the world, young boys and girls watching today will see in Kimi someone who proves that the biggest dreams can become reality."

The F1 boss then delivered the line that placed Antonelli's triumph in a longer context.

"Today, his name joins the legends of our sport," he said. "A new chapter in F1 history has been written, and I firmly believe this is only the beginning of an extraordinary legacy.

"Congratulations to Kimi, Mercedes and his family on this incredible achievement. The entire F1 community is proud to celebrate this special moment with them."

title: Lewis Hamilton demands 'serious talks' after Charles Leclerc incident fury
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has demanded "serious talks" with Ferrari after being left furious by an opening-lap incident with team-mate Charles Leclerc.

Hamilton started the Mexico City Grand Prix from pole position but fell to third by the exit of Turn 5. Leclerc gained a position on the Briton after going across the grass following a moment while the pair were side-by-side, resulting in a five-second time penalty.

The incident with Leclerc also allowed Max Verstappen to pass Hamilton, with the Dutchman going on to claim the race win after moving ahead of the Monegasque while he served his penalty.

Hamilton was furious with the penalty but did at least recover to finish second. He maximised a race restart following a red flag and overtook Leclerc, although he had no answer to Verstappen.

Despite the 41-year-old's annoyance, his immediate thoughts after the race were on Kimi Antonelli, who finished third and was crowned 2026 F1 world champion.

"Firstly, look at this crowd. We have to acknowledge them," said Hamilton.

"A huge congratulations to Kimi and the Mercedes team. It’s great to see them all up here celebrating their success.

"Youngest world champion ever, it’s pretty phenomenal, and I’m so grateful to be in the race to witness it.

"Tough day. I think we had the pace to win today, but it wasn't meant to be. We'll take it offline and see what we can do in the background."

Lewis Hamilton demands Ferrari answers after latest clash

While Hamilton was delighted for his Mercedes replacement, his words on the incident with Leclerc were clear: he was furious.

Hamilton was perplexed as to why it was only a five-second time penalty and not a 10-second punishment, and declared that the clash had cost him the win.

Asked for his thoughts on Leclerc's penalty, Hamilton responded: "In the drivers’ briefing, we discussed as soon as you go off in Turn 1, you have to give the position back. Last year I got a 10-second penalty for that same move that he did.

"But ultimately, it was that that lost us the win today. I think we have to have some serious talks behind the scenes, for sure.

"But the good thing is the team are working really hard. We’ve really improved our car. It’s great to be here, and we were on the old engine this weekend as well.

"Good results, good points. Shame we didn’t get a win, but some you win, some you lose."

title: Max Verstappen made to 'sweat' by Lewis Hamilton in fierce Mexico pursuit
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has described how he was "made to sweat" by Lewis Hamilton during their fierce late chase for Mexico City Grand Prix victory.

Starting fifth after his one place grid penalty, Verstappen was up to second place on the opening lap after passing Lewis Hamilton following his Turn 4 incident with team-mate Charles Leclerc.

Verstappen then held station behind Leclerc until the pair pitted on the same lap, with Verstappen overtaking Leclerc as he served a five-second time penalty for the Hamilton incident.

Thereafter, Verstappen led after Hamilton had pitted, with the Red Bull holding P1 throughout the red flag for Valterri Bottas's crash.

Verstappen then held onto the lead through Turns 1/2/3 against Hamilton after the standing restart, and comfortably held the Ferrari at arm's length through a late safety car for Arvid Lindblad's crash with Oscar Piastri.

It was enough to give Verstappen his third win of the season, and 74th overall, and his sixth in Mexico after 2017, 2018, 2021, 2022, and 2023.

"It was very hectic out there, but I think the first start made the race for me," said Verstappen.

"I had a very good first lap, and then we had a bit of a different strategy, but we hung in there and made the right calls at the right time.

"Of course, the penalty of Charles put us in the lead, and then you could see they were always staying with me, so it was tough.

"I was sweating at the end to try and keep Lewis behind.

"It's such a long run to Turn 1 and then to pick your breaking point there with a big bump in the middle of the track, I had to be quite careful - and then it is always a tradition in Turn 1 that two cars are fighting for the lead."

Turning to Kimi Antonelli's title glory with his third-place finish, Verstappen spoke of the 36thdriver to be champion.

"It is incredible. What a season he's had and to do that at such an age, I think, is really impressive.

"It's amazing to see the whole team celebrating with him, and his family is here as well, so I'm sure this is an emotional day, and I am very proud of him."

title: Is this the most fitting podium in Formula 1 as history made in Mexico?
excerpt:
It was a remarkable sight as two of the most decorated drivers in Formula 1 celebrated on the podium with the youngest champion in the sport's history at the end of the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Kimi Antonelli might not have won the race at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, but what he achieved was comfortably enough to set a new F1 record that may never be beaten.

The 20-year-old Italian was third at the chequered flag at the end of 71 laps, joining two of F1's greats on the rostrum.

Four-time F1 champion Max Verstappen took the chequered flag from fifth on the grid in his Red Bull, whilst polesitter Lewis Hamilton was forced to settle for second after a contentious opening lap with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.

But standing on the podium with 12 titles now between them, it was a remarkable sight.

Perhaps the most fitting podium in Formula 1 at the end of a grand prix as two generational greats stood shoulder to shoulder with a young driver joining them with such an accolade.

title: Kimi Antonelli savours 'live forever' moment after making F1 history
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli described his initial feelings in becoming Formula 1's youngest champion as something that will "live forever".

The 20-year-old Italian finished third at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez to smash the previous mark set by Sebastian Vettel by more than three years.

Antonelli joined two of the sport's greats, Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton, on the podium at the end of 71 pulsating laps.

He also ends Italy's 73 years of F1 pain in waiting for its next champion.

"We did it, we did it," exclaimed Antonelli after stepping from the cockpit his Mercedes.

"Without Mercedes, without my family, I wouldn't be here, so I'm very grateful for this moment. It will live forever. I'm speechless. I'm trying to process what has just happened."

Pointed out to Antonelli that he had Verstappen and Hamilton on the podium with him, and whether that made it even more special, he replied: "Of course, of course!

"You know it's been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max and Lewis is truly incredible. Looking forward to some more battles in the future."

Antonelli did concede to feeling "a bit more tense" this weekend, before concluding, "I'm just so happy that we got it done, and now we can enjoy the rest of the season."

title: Breaking: Kimi Antonelli smashes F1 record as youngest world champion
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has been confirmed as Formula 1's 2026 world champion, sealing the title with a third-place finish at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

The result mathematically ended the fight with four rounds still to run, with the Mercedes driver's tally now unassailable at the top of the standings.

Max Verstappen won in Mexico City, with Lewis Hamilton second and Antonelli completing the podium four seconds back.

The Italian's third place was enough, given his lead over nearest rival George Russell heading into the weekend. It sealed Antonelli's place in F1 history as the youngest world champion, breaking Sebastian Vettel's record.

Kimi Antonelli's staggering journey to the top of F1

Antonelli's route to the title began in Mercedes' junior programme, which he joined in 2019 at just 12 years old.

After sweeping European karting titles, he dominated Italian and ADAC Formula 4 in 2022 before Mercedes made the unconventional call to skip him past Formula 3 entirely, fast-tracking him into Formula 2 for 2024.

The Brackley-based squad backed that decision with an extensive testing programme in older machinery, covering roughly 9,000 kilometres across circuits including Imola, Silverstone and the Red Bull Ring to prepare him for a senior seat.

His rookie campaign in 2025 started with highlights such as Sprint pole in Miami, before a disastrous run of scoring just a single point across the European races.

However, the new power unit regulations saw a rejuvenated Antonelli, who clearly learnt hugely from his mistakes across his debut season.

Mercedes built an early technical edge with the W17 that allowed Antonelli to win five of the first six rounds, laying the foundation for his title push. In Monaco, he was untouchable in converting pole into victory.

Arguably, his highlight on his way to the world title was a statement victory at home in Monza, where he climbed from 19th on the grid to claim a staggering victory.

At the Circuit of the Americas, a one-stop strategy delivered his ninth win of the campaign at a track where Mercees were expected to struggle.

In the end, third in Mexico City was enough for Antonelli's name to be written in history. The big question: just how many titles will he go onto claim?

title: Youngest world champions in F1 history after Kimi Antonelli glory
excerpt:
Youngest world champions in F1 history

Kimi Antonelli has become the youngest F1 world champion in history by winning the 2026 title in the United States Grand Prix.

A third-place finish in the Mexico City Grand Prix was more than enough for Antonelli to be crowned the 36th F1 champion - and the youngest-ever

Antonelli is just the third Italian to be crowned world champion, and the first since Alberto Ascari in 1953.

The very first world champion, Giuseppe Farina won the 1950 title, before Ascari became the first back-to-back champion with his 1952 and 1953 successes.

Since Ascari, and before Antonelli's 2026 glory, the best an Italian had placed in the standings was Michele Alboreto in 1985 and Riccardo Patrese in 1992, whom finished as runners-up to Alain Prost, and Nigel Mansell, respectively.

Antonelli has shattered Sebastian Vettel's old record of 23 years, 4 months, 11 days by 3 years, 2 months, 11 days old, meaning he could have won the 2027, 2028 or even 2029 titles and still eclipsed the German's record from 2010.

For reference, the oldest F1 world champion was Juan Manuel Fangio in 1957, who claimed his fifth and final title after a stunning comeback drive at the German Grand Prix at the age of 46 years, 1 month, 11 days.

Antonelli would eclipse this if he won the 2052 drivers' world championship.

title: Max Verstappen survives almighty Lewis Hamilton pressure as Kimi Antonelli seals world title
excerpt:
Max Verstappen secured yet another Mexico City victory, but it is Kimi Antonelli being celebrated as the 2026 world champion.

1 November 11:25PM

Max Verstappen survived almighty late pressure from Lewis Hamilton to win the Mexico City Grand Prix, as Kimi Antonelli became Formula 1's youngest world champion.

With neither Hamilton nor George Russell winning, the title was guaranteed for Antonelli in Mexico City, yet he still managed to complete the podium.

It was a lengthy race at high altitude, following a 40-minute stoppage due to a red flag after Valtteri Bottas crashed heavily mid-race.

Charles Leclerc, who was involved in an incident with Hamilton on the first lap, finished fourth, with Lando Norris completing the top five.

Max Verstappen survives almighty Lewis Hamilton pressure as Kimi Antonelli seals world title

# Driver Team Time Tyre

Results are being loaded...

Hamilton and Leclerc have fiery opening lap clash

Unsurprisingly, all eyes were on Kimi Antonelli at the start, given what was at stake for the Mercedes driver. Crucially, almost everyone in the top 10 opted to start on softs, with the exception of Max Verstappen, who went for the mediums.

As the lights went out, Lewis Hamilton made a great start from pole position and led into the first corner, with Charles Leclerc slotting in behind. The pair battled into Turn 4, where Leclerc attempted to go around the outside.

It resulted in both Ferrari drivers going off the circuit. Leclerc cut Turn 5 completely and rejoined in the lead, while Hamilton rejoined the circuit having made the corner but slipped behind Verstappen and into third.

Behind them, it was frustration for Isack Hadjar, who was spun at Turn 6 by George Russell. Leclerc and Russell were both placed under investigation and received five- and 10-second time penalties, respectively. The leniency of the penalties left Hamilton furious.

Following the lap-one chaos, the race quickly settled, although both Aston Martins sadly retired on lap seven. What quickly became clear was how tricky it was to follow another car due to the threat of overheating.

On lap 26, Oscar Piastri was the first of the leading drivers to pit, which created a significant window for the race leaders to stop. A lap later, Leclerc and Verstappen pitted. The former served his penalty and fell behind the Dutchman as a result.

Leclerc went from softs to mediums, while Verstappen went from mediums to softs. Hamilton boxed the following lap but rejoined behind his team-mate. On lap 33, Russell pitted and served his lengthy penalty, costing him a place to Lando Norris, who pitted six laps later.

The final leading driver to pit was Antonelli, who briefly found himself in the lead but returned to fourth after pitting on lap 43. Crucially, had the Italian waited one more lap, he would have become the actual race leader.

This was because Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas suffered a scary front-left suspension failure at the first corner and crashed hard into the barrier. It initially triggered a safety car, which was quickly elevated to a full red flag on lap 45 to allow for barrier repairs.

Verstappen survives Hamilton pressure; Antonelli becomes world champion

Following barrier repairs, the Grand Prix resumed 40 minutes after Bottas' scary shunt with a standing start. Verstappen was on pole, with Leclerc, Hamilton, Antonelli and Norris completing the top five. Unsurprisingly, everyone was on soft tyres.

As the lights went out for a second time in Mexico City, Verstappen made a good start and led into the first corner. However, Hamilton was challenging him following an excellent start from the seven-time world champion.

Verstappen kept the lead through the opening corners, ahead of Hamilton and Leclerc, although Leclerc was passed by Antonelli on the following lap. Elsewhere, Oliver Bearman retired after being hit by Nico Hulkenberg, who did receive a penalty as a result.

There was a brief scare for Verstappen, who was placed under investigation on lap 50 for allegedly starting out of position, but no further action was taken.

Verstappen did well to quickly build an advantage of more than one second over Hamilton, keeping the Ferrari driver out of 'overtake mode' territory. That advantage was destroyed on lap 59, when another Safety Car was required after Arvid Lindblad crashed at Turn 2 following contact with Piastri.

The Safety Car period ended at the end of lap 62, leaving nine laps to go at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez. All eyes were on when Verstappen would restart the race. He did so on exiting the stadium section, but Hamilton remained very close.

Unfortunately for Hamilton, he could not get close enough to attack his fierce rival. Verstappen went on to hold on to the lead and claim victory, ahead of Hamilton and Antonelli, with the result securing the Italian the 2026 F1 drivers' title.

Leclerc, Norris, Russell, Piastri, Franco Colapinto, Liam Lawson, who started from the pit lane, and Pierre Gasly completed the top 10.

title: Arvid Lindblad crash leads to late-race Mexico City Grand Prix safety car
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad suffered his first in-race F1 retirement following a collision with McLaren's Oscar Piastri late in the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Running in a solid seventh position at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, Lindblad was holding off Piastri when the Australian made a move around the outside into Turn 1.

Piastri claimed Lindblad moved under braking on the approach, forcing him to attack to Lindblad's left.

Emerging out of the corner and on the short run to Turn 2, the front-right wheel of Piastri's MCL40 heavily caught the left-rear of Lindblad's VCARB03.

The contact sent Lindblad into the air before skidding across the track and into a barrier opposite Turn 2.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the stewards opted to investigate the incident.

The incident on lap 59 of the 71-lap race led to a handful of laps before racing resumed, with Red Bull's Max Verstappen leading Lewis Hamilton in his Ferrari.

title: Valtteri Bottas health update after huge Mexico GP F1 accident
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas has been released from the medical centre and is "okay" following a huge accident in the Mexico City Grand Prix.

On his 43rd lap, as the Finn applied the brakes for Turn 1 at maximum speed, he suffered a front-left suspension failure, which meant he lost control of the Cadillac.

Fortunately, the car went into the TecPro barriers rear first and not broadside or head-first, which minimised some of the impact for the 10-time grand prix winner.

Medical personnel and an ambulance were deployed, although Bottas was able to climb from the car himself before going off for a medical check.

After this, the team provided a medical update on his condition.

"Following a precautionary medical assessment, Valtteri Bottas has been released and is okay," read a team statement.

"He has been excused from all post-race media duties, including the TV pen and written media pen."

Cadillac also pledged to "investigate the on-track incident fully" after Bottas's failure.

title: Max Verstappen radio dismissed as FIA stewards explain Charles Leclerc penalty
excerpt:
The FIA stewards have explained their thinking behind Charles Leclerc's Mexico City Grand Prix penalty, which appeared to go against the grain of their guidelines.

Leclerc was handed a five-second penalty for an opening-lap squabble with Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton at the Autodrómo Hermanos Rodríguez.

The Monégasque was adjudged to have left the track and gained a lasting advantage as he had been second heading into Turn 4, but emerged with the lead as Hamilton also ran wide.

Despite guidelines from the stewards to the teams and drivers pre-race that such incidents would incur a penalty if they did not give the gained positions back by a certain point later in the lap, Leclerc carried on out front.

When the stewards finally delivered their verdict, and upon being informed of a seemingly lesser penalty, Verstappen said: Ha! I thought all the new penalties were 10 [seconds]."

Via a statement, the stewards made clear why the penalty was eventually halved.

"The stewards have determined that both cars entered Turn 4 with excessive speed and therefore neither would have been able to make the corner on track, as demonstrated by the fact that car 44 [Hamilton], which was on the inside, had to go off track to make the corner," read the statement.

"Car 16 was therefore not entitled to claim the corner due to the excessive entry speed.

"The driver then completed an overtake whilst off track, and accordingly this warrants a penalty.

"The baseline penalty guideline is 10 seconds; however, in mitigation is the fact that car 44 was also off track on the inside of car 16, and this occurred early in the first lap."

title: Frightening Valtteri Bottas crash sparks Mexico City GP red flag
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas suffered a frightening high-speed crash in the Mexico City Grand Prix that brought the race to a halt.

On lap 44 of the 71-lap race at the Autodrómo Hermanos Rodríguez, and hurtling along the main straight into Turn 1, Bottas' Cadillac suffered a front-left suspension failure, with his car travelling at 320kph.

As the car immediately bottomed out, and as Bottas hit the brakes, it brought up a shower of sparks, leaving the Finn a passenger as the barrier loomed large.

A slight spin resulted in Bottas hitting the barrier with the rear-wing first. Clearly winded, it took Bottas a while before he finally gave the thumbs up to signal he was okay.

With the Cadillac embedded in the barrier, FIA race director Rui Marques had no choice but to red flag the race to allow repairs to the barrier to be carried.

At the time of the stoppage, Red Bull's Max Verstappen led from Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, followed by Kimi Antonelli in his Mercedes and the second SF-26 of Lewis Hamilton.
